questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had always wanted to visit Japan, as I have always had an interest in their culture. And I have never lived in another country before. Therefore a semester abroad in Japan seemed like a match made in heaven.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Well, all the information is there, but it can be a bit tricky to find, as Waseda sends a whole lot of documents (some of them important, a lot of them less so) around the beginning of the stay and navigating their website is no cakewalk either, as it is filled with a whole lot of pages. So not exactly easy, but not too bad.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Waseda University sends most of the information you need before you even arrive. And they host some in-person information events prior to the start of classes, that were pretty helpful as well.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Waseda University has 3 dorms right next to campus - I applied for them all and was lucky enough to get a spot at the one called Waseda Hoshien.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: No meal plans in any of Waseda's own dorms - there was a shared kitchen on each floor of the dorm, with sufficient facilities in my opinion.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It might be a bit more expensive than other housing options, but it is very practical to live right next to campus, not having to commute.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Speaking location, price point and facilities, I was very satisfied. The dorm was clean and quiet, which is a good thing of course. However, I was a bit disappointed how little the dorm invited social life, even within the dorm. You are not allowed to invite guests over (only family members are allowed to even visit your room, and only for 30 minutes!!) and the common areas in the building (at least in my building) are not designed to be hangout spots the way you would expect them to be in a Danish dorm - e.g. the kitchen consists of individual single-person desks ... there is one common area more specifically designed for social interaction I think, but I never really got to use this, and I don't know if it was used all that often - the dorm did n't do a whole lot for us to get acquainted with each other.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: As has already been described by many others, the course registration is one big lottery consisting of three rounds of registration - do not expect to get the courses you set out to get. And the digital system in which you apply is very old school, not in a good way.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Very limited to be frank - I spoke to the SILS office once or twice to help me sort out some issues I had.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: In the end I got most of what I wanted, but I also had to give up one/two courses I really wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be open to do some courses you might not would have thought to do initially - the one I enjoyed the most was a more or less random choice for me.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
VERY IMPORTANT SIDENOTE!!!

DO NOT ENROLL IN SILS IF YOU DO NOT ALREADY STUDY JAPANESE - this caused me a lot of trouble as Japanese courses are mandatory at SILS, and seeing as I don't study it, I had to beginner courses that I couldn't get approved by UCPH - neither Waseda or UCPH are flexible in a case like this, and so I had to write an extracurricular exam for UCPH whilst abroad which was very stressful! And to be frank I don't think either part is doing a very good job at informing exchange students about this very important detail at SILS - I only found out when it was too late to apply for another one of the Waseda schools.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Very much like highschool - not the academic level I was used to from my BA at UCPH, and way too much homework. The reason I am giving it a relatively low satisfaction score has some to do with this, but also has very much to do with some very lackluster teaching I got from a couple of the professors.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching was not all that different, it was just way more homework, and a lot of it was not properly integrated in the face-to-face lectures.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- History of English Literature　01
- Music and Musicology
- Python Programming for Digital Humanities　01
- Video Game Studies　01
- Nihongo 1 (1)
- Japanese for 'zero' beginners

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would highly recommend History of English Literature (or any other courses taught by Professor Tsukada). It was a very insightful an engaging, and the professor is very passionate and entertaining. I really enjoyed this course!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The National Healthcare; it wasn't unexpected but it was a bit more cumbersome than I thought to sign up for and to pay for. Very bureaucratic process.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Most things were very cheap, compared to Copenhagen at least, as the yen is quite weak at the moment.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Didn't attend any.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not too sure - a lot of them didn't seem suitable for international students, as you needed to be somewhat fluent in Japanese to attend. There is one I heard of, which was designed for international students, that was kind of a cultural exchange type of thing. Waseda Paddy it's called.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
- Get out of the city every once in a while - Tokyo is a very busy and crowded place, so it is very nice to do daytrips outside the city, seeing some more quiet parts of Japan.

- Explore some of the many wonderful (and cheap!) food-places in around.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Ok, just going to continue the list above here, hehe.

- Go to a public bath (sento), preferrably one on the outskirts of the city, as they can be quite busy in the city. If you get the chance, please try onsen as well!

- Read a book, and have a cold drink in a nearby park (watch out for crows though, I actually was attacked by one one time, haha). Or tag a friend along and throw a frisbee and eat ice cream :))

- Hike a mountain.

- Go visit an arcade with a friend.

- Travel the country; I went to Hokkaido (Sapporo and Hakodate) which was an absolute blast.

- Visit Meguro Cinema: they have English movies every now and then, and it's a pretty cool spot.

- Visit Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building in Shinjuku: tall building with an amazing view over city, and it's doesn't cost anything to go there.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Not easy, that's for sure. Culture shock was more significant for me than I had expected: language barrier and a plethora of unwritten rules  can make be very overwhelming in the beginning.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Not really, I didn't really make any local friends ...

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language for sure - lots of people do not speak English.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciated how everything just sort of works here; trains are on time, people respect each other when standing in line, public spaces are clean etc. People are very conscious that they are part of a bigger whole, and have to behave appropriately, which is what makes it all possible <33

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Be prepared that going on exchange is going to be challenging: personally I had way more culture shock than expected, felt way lonelier than expected and missed my friends and family each and every day. Bummer message, I know, but I don't think the general idea of what a semester abroad looks like is representative of the challenges.

- Be curious and open-minded and make sure to not stall in your stay --> visit all places you might find interesting, eat something new. 9 times out of 10 these excursions, however tiny, will be worth it :))

- Make absolutely sure the school you're enrolling in can secure all the ECTS credits you need. As previously stated, SILS is not for students that are not already studying Japanese.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you're looking for something liberal artsy, and you don't already study Japanese, don't go to Waseda University, go for Tokyo University instead. And think carefully about whether Tokyo is the right place for you - I was very overwhelmed by the big-city-living, and think I would have actually prefered to go for a quieter town in Japan, if I had to change anything.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: As much as I was overwhelmed by culture chock, the challenges have made me learn a lot of things about myself. Ultimately, I think it's pretty healthy to get out of your comfort zone every now and then.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Keeping my spirits up - sometimes when the academic challenges and my homesickness got to me, I had a hard time seeing the point in studying abroad in the first place.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
DO NOT ENROLL IN SILS IF YOU ARE NOT STUDYING JAPANESE:

Waseda and UCPH will not help you if you cannot get enough credits secured through English-taught courses. I had to spent way more time than I should have just figuring out a solution, and the solution was a very far from ideal.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
